items.title: New Hampshire Right to Privacy Act — Notification of Security Breach Required
items.citation: RSA 359-C:19 to 359-C:21 (vendor duty at RSA 359-C:20, II)
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any person or business that maintains computerized data that includes personal information that the person or business does not own shall notify and cooperate with the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the data immediately following discovery." The owner/licensee then determines whether notice to individuals is required.
key_obligations: Owner/licensee of computerized personal data must, on becoming aware of a breach, promptly determine the likelihood of misuse and notify affected individuals "as soon as possible" if misuse occurred/is likely or cannot be ruled out
A non-owning maintainer (vendor) must notify and cooperate with the owner/licensee "immediately following discovery" of the breach
Entities regulated under RSA 358-A:3, I notify their primary regulator; all others notify the NH Attorney General
Notice to over 1,000 consumers requires notifying nationwide consumer reporting agencies "without unreasonable delay"
Required notice content includes a general description of the incident, approximate breach date, type of personal information involved, and contact information
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as possible" (to individuals); "immediately following discovery" (vendor/maintainer to owner or licensee)
items.regulator_notice: Primary regulator (if regulated under RSA 358-A:3, I) or the NH Attorney General otherwise; no explicit numeric resident-count threshold found in the fetched text
items.personal_info_definition_notes: The fetched statutory text references "computerized data that includes personal information" without an explicit standalone definition in RSA 359-C:20 itself
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official gc.nh.gov text of RSA 359-C:20 and confirmed the vendor-to-owner duty, timing, and regulator-notice structure. No penalty provision or personal-information definition appeared in this specific section; did not fetch RSA 359-C:19 (definitions) or RSA 359-C:21 (enforcement) separately this session, so penalties are left null rather than guessed.

items.title: Student Online Personal Information
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds "operators" — the operator of an internet website, online service, online application, or mobile application with actual knowledge that it is used primarily for, and designed and marketed for, K-12 school purposes. LOVELEEDAY would qualify as an operator for any K-12-marketed product.
key_obligations: Operators may not engage in targeted advertising on their own site/service/application, or elsewhere, based on covered student information
Operators may not use covered information to amass a profile about a K-12 student
Operators may not sell, lease, rent, trade, or otherwise make available a student's information
Operators may not disclose protected information except in response to judicial process
The section explicitly does not impose a compliance-review/enforcement duty on electronic store/marketplace or interactive-computer-service providers regarding third-party content providers
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Governs "covered information" tied to K-12 student use of an operator's site/service/application; full definitions section (RSA 189:65-68) not independently fetched this session
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official gc.nh.gov text of RSA 189:68-a directly; no enforcement/penalty provision appeared in this section's text, so left null rather than guessed. Did not independently fetch the surrounding definitions sections (RSA 189:65-68).

items.title: New Hampshire Privacy Act (Expectation of Privacy)
items.citation: RSA 507-H (applicability RSA 507-H:2, I; processor duties RSA 507-H:7, II; enforcement RSA 507-H:11)
items.applies_to_vendor: RSA 507-H:7, II sets direct statutory obligations on "processors" (vendors acting on a controller's behalf) — LOVELEEDAY would be a processor for most client engagements under this Act.
key_obligations: Applies to entities conducting business in NH that during a one-year period process personal data of not less than 35,000 unique consumers (excluding payment-only transactions), or process data of not less than 10,000 unique consumers and derive more than 25% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data (RSA 507-H:2, I)

Processors must act under a binding contract with the controller setting out processing instructions, nature/purpose of processing, data types, duration, and the rights/obligations of both parties (RSA 507-H:7, II)
Processor staff must be bound by confidentiality agreements
Processors must delete or return data to the controller on request unless retention is legally required
Processors must engage subcontractors only under a further written contract and make compliance documentation available to the controller for assessment
items.regulator_notice: Exclusive enforcement authority rests with the NH Attorney General (RSA 507-H:11, I); violations are treated as an unfair or deceptive act/practice under RSA 358-A:2; no private right of action (RSA 507-H:11, IV-V); a 60-day cure period was mandatory during 2025 and becomes discretionary after 2026
items.penalties: Enforced as an RSA 358-A unfair/deceptive trade practice by the Attorney General; specific civil penalty dollar amounts were not shown in the fetched text
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official gc.nh.gov merged chapter text and confirmed applicability thresholds, processor obligations, and enforcement structure directly.

items.title: Identity Theft Prevention Act — Disclosure of breach of security to customers
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any business or public entity that compiles or maintains computerized records that include personal information on behalf of another business or public entity shall notify that business or public entity...of any breach of the security of the system." LOVELEEDAY, as the party maintaining client records, must notify its client (the data owner), who then handles consumer-facing notice.
key_obligations: A business conducting business in NJ, or a public entity that compiles/maintains computerized personal-information records, must disclose a breach to affected NJ-resident customers following discovery
A business/public entity that maintains records on behalf of another business or public entity (i.e., a vendor) must notify that other business/entity of any breach
Notification of more than 1,000 persons at one time triggers a duty to notify, without unreasonable delay, all nationwide consumer reporting agencies
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement...or any measures necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore the reasonable integrity of the data system"
items.personal_info_definition_notes: An individual's first name/initial and last name combined with: (1) Social Security number; (2) driver's license or State ID number; or (3) account, credit, or debit card number in combination with any required security code. "Breach of security" excludes access to encrypted or otherwise unreadable data.
items.effective_or_amended: Original enactment P.L.2005, c.226; per secondary sources, amended by P.L.2019, c.95 to add categories such as biometric data and online-account username/email plus password — this amendment was not independently confirmed against an official NJ text this session
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official pub.njleg.gov text of P.L.2005, c.226 (the original enacting law codified at N.J.S.A. 56:8-163) and confirmed the vendor-to-owner duty, timing, and CRA threshold. Did not independently fetch the 2019 amendment (P.L.2019, c.95) text, so the expanded personal-information definition and any penalty provision it may have added are not confirmed here — flagged rather than guessed.

No enacted, dedicated SOPIPA-style NJ student-data-privacy statute binding operators/vendors could be confirmed. Checked: (1) N.J.S.A. Title 18A, Chapter 36, which contains parental-consent provisions for school surveys and internet disclosure of student information (18A:36-34, 18A:36-35) but is not a comprehensive operator/vendor data-privacy statute; (2) a bill titled the "Student Digital Privacy and Parental Rights Act" (S794 / A1272 / A3936, 2014-2016 sessions, supplementing Title 18A Chapter 36) — only introduced-version bill text was found on pub.njleg.gov, with no confirmed Public Law chapter number or codified N.J.S.A. section; (3) the official NJ Student Data System privacy page (njsds.nj.gov) and an NJSBA legal explainer, neither of which cites any NJ-specific student-privacy statute, only FERPA/PPRA/COPPA/CIPA; (4) non-official marketing sources claim an enacted "SOPPA-NJ"/"A4978" but their own citation resolves to P.L.2023, c.266 (S332), which is the general New Jersey Data Protection Act (a comprehensive consumer privacy law), not a K-12-specific statute. Given the never-fabricate rule, this is recorded as exists:false rather than guessing a citation.

items.title: New Jersey Data Protection Act (NJDPA)
items.citation: P.L.2023, c.266 (S332); codified in N.J.S.A. Title 56 (exact section numbers not independently confirmed this session)
items.applies_to_vendor: Establishes controller/processor roles; processors (vendors, such as LOVELEEDAY, handling data on behalf of a controller client) must operate under a data processing agreement and implement required security measures.
key_obligations: Establishes controller and processor roles with written data-processing-agreement requirements between them
Requires reasonable security measures appropriate to the sensitivity/scope of personal data
Requires data protection assessments for higher-risk processing activities (per secondary sources; not independently confirmed from the official text this session)

items.title: Data Breach Notification Act
items.citation: NMSA 1978, §§ 57-12C-1 to 57-12C-12 (vendor duty and consumer notice at § 57-12C-6; AG/CRA notice at § 57-12C-10; contractual security flow-down at § 57-12C-5)
items.applies_to_vendor: Section 57-12C-6 includes a duty for a person who maintains computerized data containing a NM resident's personal identifying information that the person does not own or license to notify the owner or licensee of a breach. Separately, § 57-12C-5 requires anyone disclosing personal identifying information to a service provider under contract to require by contract that the provider implement reasonable security procedures — a direct flow-down obligation onto vendors like LOVELEEDAY.
key_obligations: A person who owns or licenses NM residents' personal identifying information must notify each affected resident "in the most expedient time possible, but not later than forty-five calendar days following discovery of the security breach"
A person maintaining but not owning such data must notify the owner/licensee of a breach
Notification is not required if an investigation determines the breach does not give rise to a significant risk of identity theft or fraud
Breaches requiring notice to more than 1,000 NM residents also require notice to the NM Attorney General and nationwide consumer reporting agencies, within the same 45-day window
Contracts disclosing personal identifying information to a service provider must contractually require the provider to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible, but not later than forty-five calendar days following discovery of the security breach"
items.regulator_notice: NM Attorney General and nationwide consumer reporting agencies, required once notice is owed to more than 1,000 New Mexico residents
items.uncertainty: nmonesource.com (New Mexico's official Compilation Commission publisher) returned 403/blocked responses to direct WebFetch attempts this session, so the official text could not be independently rendered. Content above (sections 57-12C-4, -5, -6, -10) was cross-checked against codes.findlaw.com and law.justia.com, both secondary sources, not the source_url. Penalty provisions (§ 57-12C-11/12) were not located this session and are left null rather than guessed.

No enacted New Mexico SOPIPA-style student-data-privacy statute binding operators/vendors was found. Checked: the NM Data Breach Notification Act (NMSA 57-12C), which is security-only and not student-specific; the NM Public School Code (Chapter 22) index for a dedicated student-privacy operator statute; the Parent Coalition for Student Privacy's state legislation tracker, which does not list New Mexico among states with a comprehensive student-privacy law; and an official NM Public Education Department guidance document, which frames student-data protection in New Mexico around federal FERPA rather than a state operator statute. This session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before an exhaustive statute-by-statute search of NMSA Chapter 22 could be completed, so this should be treated as a strong but not certain negative.

New Mexico has no enacted comprehensive consumer privacy law. Senate Bill 176 (2019), the "Consumer Information Privacy Act," was introduced on the official nmlegis.gov site (fetched as source_url, confirming the bill's existence as introduced text) but was reported by a secondary compliance tracker (centraleyes.com) as "postponed indefinitely," which was not independently re-confirmed against an official NM Legislature bill-status page this session because the WebSearch budget was exhausted.

items.title: Identity Theft Protection Act — Protection from security breaches
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any business that maintains or possesses records or data containing personal information of a resident of North Carolina that the business does not own or license...shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any security breach immediately following discovery of the breach."
key_obligations: A business that owns/licenses NC resident personal information, or conducts business in NC and owns/licenses such information in any form, must notify affected persons following discovery of a breach
A business that maintains/possesses records containing personal information it does not own must notify the owner/licensee "immediately following discovery of the breach"
The NC Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division must be notified whenever notice is given to an affected person, and in particular whenever a breach affects more than 1,000 persons at one time
Law-enforcement delay is available on written request, with notice required thereafter without unreasonable delay
items.notice_deadline: "without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement" (general obligation); "immediately following discovery of the breach" (non-owning business to owner/licensee) — no fixed number of days is set in the statute
items.regulator_notice: NC Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division — required whenever consumer notice is given, and specifically when more than 1,000 persons are affected at one time
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Applies to personal information "in any form (whether computerized, paper, or otherwise)"; excludes email addresses, internet/online account numbers, and passwords (unless permitting access to a financial account), and electronic identification numbers
items.penalties: A violation is a violation of N.C.G.S. § 75-1.1 (unfair or deceptive trade practices), enforced by the Attorney General; a private right of action exists only for an individual actually injured by the violation
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official ncleg.net text of G.S. 75-65 directly and confirmed the vendor duty, timing language, AG threshold, penalty structure, and personal-information definition.

items.title: Student Online Personal Information Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies directly to "operators" of a website, online service, online application, or mobile application with knowledge that it is used primarily for, and was designed and marketed for, K-12 school purposes.
key_obligations: Operators may not engage in targeted advertising on their own site/service/application, or elsewhere, using information gathered through K-12 school use
Operators may not amass a profile about a student except in furtherance of K-12 school purposes
Operators may not sell or rent a student's information, including covered information, with narrow exceptions (e.g., business acquisitions, or assessment providers with express written consent)
Operators must restrict disclosure of covered information to permitted purposes (K-12 school purposes, legal compliance, safety, or contracted services under confidentiality requirements)

A parent, K-12 school, teacher, local board of education, or the State Board of Education may report an alleged violation to the Attorney General, who may bring a civil action for injunctive relief; the statute creates no private right of action
items.regulator_notice: NC Attorney General, via complaint referral; injunctive relief only
items.penalties: No statutory monetary penalty found; enforcement is limited to AG-sought injunctive relief, with no private right of action
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official ncleg.net text of G.S. 115C-401.2 directly and confirmed the operator prohibitions and enforcement mechanism. A related but distinct statute, G.S. 115C-402.5, governs student-data handling by NC state/local education agencies themselves (not primarily operators/vendors) and was not used as the basis for this item.

No comprehensive NC consumer data privacy law (CCPA/VCDPA-style) was found. The official NC Department of Justice security-breach page (fetched) describes only the Identity Theft Protection Act's breach-notification duties and does not reference any broader consumer-privacy statute. This is an absence-of-mention on that specific page rather than an explicit official statement that no such law exists; this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before the NC General Assembly's current-session bill tracker could be checked directly for a recently passed comprehensive privacy act.

items.title: Notice of Security Breach for Personal Information
items.citation: N.D.C.C. ch. 51-30 (§§ 51-30-01 to 51-30-07; vendor duty at § 51-30-03; AG/consumer notice at § 51-30-02; enforcement at § 51-30-07)
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any person that maintains computerized data that includes personal information that the person does not own shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of the breach of the security of the data immediately following the discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person."
key_obligations: A person/business owning or licensing computerized personal data must notify affected ND residents in the most expedient manner possible following discovery of a breach
A person maintaining data it does not own must notify the owner or licensee "immediately following the discovery"
The ND Attorney General must be notified when a breach affects more than 250 ND residents
The Attorney General enforces the chapter using the powers and remedies available under N.D.C.C. ch. 51-15 (consumer fraud)
items.notice_deadline: "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" (owner to residents/AG); "immediately following the discovery" (non-owning maintainer to owner/licensee)
items.regulator_notice: ND Attorney General, required when a breach affects more than 250 individuals
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Breach of the security system" means unauthorized acquisition of computerized data where access has not been secured by encryption or another rendering-unreadable technology; good-faith acquisition by an employee/agent is not a breach if the information is not further used or disclosed
items.uncertainty: The official ndlegis.gov chapter page confirms the chapter's section structure (51-30-01 through 51-30-07), but its linked PDF returned compressed/undecodable text this session, so the specific statutory language quoted above was cross-checked against codes.findlaw.com (secondary), not read directly from the official PDF. No specific civil-penalty dollar figure could be located in § 51-30-07 itself (it only references ch. 51-15 remedies generally), so penalties is left null rather than guessed.

items.title: Protection of student data — school district policy
items.applies_to_vendor: Governs school districts rather than vendors directly: it requires a district board to adopt a student-data-protection policy and to obtain board permission before student data is shared with any non-employee or external entity — which in practice sets the gate LOVELEEDAY must clear (a board-approved data-sharing agreement) to receive ND student data as a vendor. 2025 H.B. 1357 adds a mandatory data-sharing agreement between the district and the state Department of Public Instruction.
key_obligations: Each school district board must adopt a policy on protection of student data
The district must obtain board permission before sharing student data with any non-employee or external entity (subject to exceptions for parents and legally required disclosures)
The superintendent must compile and maintain a list of all individuals/entities receiving student data, and a list, by title, of district personnel with data access
The district must make the policy available upon request
Per 2025 H.B. 1357, districts must execute a data-sharing agreement with the state Department of Public Instruction
items.uncertainty: The official ndlegis.gov chapter page and PDF did not render readable section text this session (PDF returned compressed/undecodable content); the statutory language above was cross-checked against codes.findlaw.com (secondary). This is a school-district-policy statute rather than a direct operator/vendor conduct statute like NH/NC's SOPIPA-style laws — flagged since it is the closest ND analog found, not a perfect match to the BRIEF's SOPIPA example.

Fetched the official North Dakota Attorney General site; its consumer-protection navigation covers identity theft, scams, and credit freezes but references no comprehensive consumer data privacy statute. Consistent with North Dakota's 2023 comprehensive-privacy bill (H.B. 1127) having failed to pass, though this session's exhausted WebSearch budget prevented independently re-confirming the current 2025-2026 legislative session status.

items.title: Private disclosure of security breach of computerized personal information data
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any person that...is the custodian of or stores computerized data...on behalf of another person or governmental entity, shall notify that other person or governmental entity of any breach of the security of the system...in an expeditious manner."
key_obligations: A person that owns or licenses computerized personal information must disclose any breach that compromises security and is reasonably likely to result in identity theft or fraud
A person that is only the custodian/storage provider of the data (i.e., a vendor) must notify the owning person or governmental entity of a breach "in an expeditious manner"
Notice to affected Ohio residents must occur in the most expedient time possible, not later than 45 days following discovery

Breaches affecting more than 1,000 Ohio residents at once trigger a duty to notify, without unreasonable delay, all nationwide consumer reporting agencies of the timing, distribution, and content of the disclosure
An encryption safe harbor applies where encryption keys were not also compromised
The Attorney General may investigate and bring a civil action for a person's alleged failure to comply
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible but not later than forty-five days following its discovery or notification of the breach"
items.regulator_notice: No separate AG notice threshold found in the fetched text beyond the AG's general investigation/civil-action authority; nationwide CRA notice required above 1,000 affected residents
items.personal_info_definition_notes: An individual's name combined with Social Security number, driver's license/State ID number, or account/card number "in combination with and linked to any required security code, access code, or password"; excludes publicly available information and information lawfully disseminated through news media or directories
items.penalties: Enforced via Attorney General civil action; no specific statutory dollar penalty was found in the fetched text of this section
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official codes.ohio.gov text of ORC 1349.19 directly and confirmed the vendor/custodian duty, 45-day deadline, CRA threshold, safe harbor, and personal-information definition. The section's original enactment/effective date was not shown in the fetched text itself, so left null rather than guessed (secondary sources place original enactment in 2006, effective 2007).

items.title: Student data privacy — technology provider requirements
items.citation: Ohio Rev. Code § 3319.326 (enacted by 2024 Senate Bill 29)
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies directly to "technology providers" — any entity contracting with an Ohio school district regarding education records — placing LOVELEEDAY under statutory duties as if it were the district itself.
key_obligations: A technology provider shall not sell, share, or disseminate education records except as provided by the section or under a valid delegation/assignment of its district contract
A technology provider shall not use education records for any commercial purpose, including marketing or advertising to a student or parent
A technology provider may use de-identified aggregate student information only to improve, maintain, develop, support, or diagnose its own website, service, or operations
Contracts must restrict data access to employees/contractors fulfilling official duties
A technology provider must comply with Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 1347 regarding collection, use, and protection of data "as if it were a school district," including breach reporting under § 1347.12
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official codes.ohio.gov text of ORC 3319.326 directly and confirmed the technology-provider restrictions and Chapter 1347 flow-down. No standalone enforcement/penalty clause was found within this section itself.

No comprehensive Ohio consumer data privacy law (beyond breach notification under ORC 1349.19 and the voluntary Data Protection Act safe harbor under ORC 1354) was found. The official Ohio Attorney General homepage (fetched) does not reference one. A direct attempt to check the Ohio Legislature's bill tracker for the repeatedly-introduced "Ohio Personal Privacy Act" failed on a TLS certificate error, and this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before an alternate check could be made, so current-session enactment status could not be independently re-confirmed.

items.title: Notification; person without valid authorization has acquired private information
items.applies_to_vendor: "Any person or business which maintains computerized data which includes private information which such person or business does not own shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach" — notice to the owner must be made immediately, and in any case within thirty days following discovery.
key_obligations: An owner/licensee of computerized private data must disclose a breach to affected NY residents in the most expedient time possible, within 30 days after discovery
A non-owning maintainer (vendor) must notify the owner/licensee immediately, and in any case within 30 days following discovery
The Attorney General and relevant state agencies must be notified of any breach affecting NY residents, including timing, content, distribution, and approximate number affected
Nationwide consumer reporting agencies must be notified when more than 5,000 NY residents are to be notified at one time
Notice may be delayed at the request of law enforcement
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, provided that such notification shall be made within thirty days after the breach has been discovered" (to residents); "immediately, provided that such notification shall be made within thirty days following discovery" (vendor to owner)
items.regulator_notice: NY Attorney General and relevant state agencies, for any number of affected NY residents; nationwide consumer reporting agencies once more than 5,000 residents are to be notified at one time
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Private information" includes personal information combined with Social Security number, driver's license number, financial account number with security code, biometric data, medical/health insurance information, or an online account username/email address combined with a password or security question and answer
items.penalties: For knowing or reckless violations: the greater of $5,000 or up to $20 per instance of failed notification, capped at $250,000
items.effective_or_amended: Amended February 14, 2025 to clarify which businesses must additionally notify NYDFS as covered entities (per secondary source; not independently re-verified against the amendment text this session)
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official nysenate.gov text of GBL 899-aa directly and confirmed vendor duty, timing, thresholds, and penalties. The February 2025 NYDFS-related amendment is noted from a secondary source and was not independently re-fetched against the amended statutory text this session.

items.title: Data protection and student privacy — third-party contractor obligations
items.citation: Education Law § 2-d; implementing regulations at 8 NYCRR Part 121
items.applies_to_vendor: A "third-party contractor" is "any person or entity, other than an educational agency, that receives student data or teacher or principal data from an educational agency pursuant to a contract or other written agreement for purposes of providing services" — this is the category LOVELEEDAY falls into when contracting with a NY school/district.
key_obligations: Contracts with third-party contractors must include a data security and privacy plan detailing implementation of all applicable data-security/privacy requirements over the contract's life
Contractors must limit internal access to education records to individuals with legitimate educational interests
Contractors must not use education records for purposes beyond those explicitly authorized in the contract
Contractors must maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, and use encryption to protect data in motion and in custody
Contractors must notify the educational agency of any unauthorized release of student/teacher/principal data in the most expedient way possible and without unreasonable delay
items.notice_deadline: Breach/unauthorized-release notice to the educational agency: "the most expedient way possible and without unreasonable delay"
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Covers student data and APPR (teacher/principal) data specifically, distinct from GBL's general "private information" definition
items.penalties: Civil penalties against a contractor: up to $1,000 for a first violation, up to $5,000 for a second violation involving the same data, up to $10,000 for subsequent violations; for a breach, the greater of $5,000 or up to $10 per affected individual
items.effective_or_amended: Part 121 regulations adopted by the Board of Regents January 14, 2020; effective January 29, 2020 (per secondary source, not independently re-fetched this session)
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official nysenate.gov text of Education Law 2-d directly and confirmed the third-party-contractor definition, required contract terms, and penalty tiers. Part 121's adoption/effective dates are cited from NYSED's own counsel page (an official state-agency source) but were not independently re-fetched this session, so flagged as secondary-sourced.

New York has not enacted a comprehensive consumer data privacy law comparable to the VCDPA/CCPA model; the repeatedly-introduced New York Privacy Act (S365 and successors) has not passed as of this research. The official NY Attorney General homepage (fetched) contains no reference to such a law, only a data-breach-reporting resource. This session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before the current 2025-2026 legislative session's bill status could be independently re-confirmed, so this is recorded as a strong but not freshly re-verified negative.

items.title: SHIELD Act — reasonable data security safeguards requirement
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to "any person or business that owns or licenses computerized data which includes private information of a resident of New York" — a broad standard that reaches a vendor like LOVELEEDAY whenever it holds NY-resident private information for its own operational purposes (e.g., as a controller of its own client/vendor records), and which independently requires any covered business to oversee its own service providers' safeguards by contract.
key_obligations: Must develop, implement, and maintain a data security program with reasonable administrative safeguards: designate employee(s) to coordinate the program, identify reasonably foreseeable internal/external risks, train employees, require safeguards from service providers by contract, and adjust the program as the business changes

Must implement reasonable technical safeguards: assess risk in network/software design and in information processing, transmission, and storage; detect, prevent, and respond to attacks; regularly test and monitor controls

Must implement reasonable physical safeguards: assess risk of information storage/disposal, detect/prevent/respond to intrusions, protect against unauthorized access, and dispose of data so it cannot be read or reconstructed
Small businesses (fewer than 50 employees, under $3M annual revenue, or under $5M in assets) must implement safeguards "appropriate for the size and complexity" of their own operations
Violations are treated as a GBL § 349 violation, enforceable by the Attorney General for injunctive relief and civil penalties under § 350-d; the section creates no private right of action
items.regulator_notice: NY Attorney General enforcement under GBL §§ 349/350-d; no specific resident-count notice threshold (this is a safeguards duty, not a breach-notice duty)
items.penalties: AG-sought injunctive relief and civil penalties under GBL § 350-d; no private right of action
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official nysenate.gov text of GBL 899-bb directly and confirmed the administrative/technical/physical safeguard requirements, small-business scaling, and enforcement mechanism.
